title: Roadmap 13: NoSQL, Redis, consistency theory and vectors
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: MongoDB document modelling, Redis caching and its lock caveats, CAP/PACELC and consistency models, columnar warehouses, and vector search with pgvector.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: An order always has between 1 and 30 line items, which are almost always read together with the order and rarely queried on their own. How should this be modelled in MongoDB?

options.text: Embed the line items as an array inside the order document.
options.why: Right: one read returns everything and the array size is small and bounded.

options.text: Store each line item in its own collection and look them up one by one.
options.why: Forces extra queries or $lookup for data that is always read together.

options.text: Keep only item ids in the order and join them with $lookup on every read.
options.why: Adds join-like work to the hottest read path for no isolation benefit.

options.text: Put the whole order in Redis and write it to MongoDB once a day.
options.why: Adds a second store and risks losing data; it does not address modelling.

questions.explanation: Embed when data is read together, owned by the parent and bounded in size. Reference when the child grows without limit, is shared, or is queried independently.

questions.prompt: A hot cached product page has a 5 minute TTL. Each time it expires, thousands of requests miss at once and hit the database. What is the best mitigation?

options.text: Let one request rebuild each key while others wait or serve stale data; add TTL jitter.
options.why: Right: single-flight collapses the herd and jitter spreads expiries.

options.text: Raise the TTL on every key to one whole day so that expiry becomes rare and the herd is avoided.
options.why: Only delays the problem and serves staler data everywhere.

options.text: Turn off TTLs and rely on LRU eviction to eventually remove the old product pages.
options.why: Eviction is not invalidation, so stale data can live indefinitely.

options.text: Add more database read replicas and let every miss query the database.
options.why: Absorbs some load but the herd still hits the database on every expiry.

questions.explanation: A cache stampede is many concurrent misses for one key. Fix it with a per-key lock or single-flight, stale-while-revalidate, early refresh and TTL jitter.

questions.prompt: True or false: a single SET key token NX EX lock in Redis guarantees mutual exclusion even if the primary fails over to an asynchronous replica.

options.text: True
options.why: Replication is asynchronous, so a promoted replica may not have the lock key.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the primary can grant the lock and die before replicating it, so a second client can acquire it.

questions.explanation: Use a Redis lock as an efficiency tool. When correctness matters, enforce the invariant in the database (conditional update, version column) or use a fencing token.

questions.prompt: Select all statements about PACELC that are correct.

options.text: It extends CAP: if there is a partition choose availability or consistency, else choose latency or consistency.
options.why: Right: the "else" half is the contribution beyond CAP.

options.text: A PC/EC system favours consistency both during partitions and when the network is healthy.
options.why: Right: it pays in availability and latency to stay consistent.

options.text: Partition tolerance can be skipped if the servers sit in one reliable data centre.
options.why: Networks and processes can still partition or stall; P is not optional.

options.text: It says every consistent system is slower than an eventually consistent one in all cases.
options.why: The trade-off is about replication coordination, not an absolute speed rule.

options.text: It replaces the C in CAP with durability when the network is healthy.
options.why: The E branch still concerns consistency versus latency, not durability.

questions.explanation: CAP only describes behaviour during a partition. PACELC adds the everyday trade-off: waiting for replicas (consistency) versus answering fast (latency).

questions.prompt: True or false: read-your-writes consistency can hold for a client even when the system as a whole is only eventually consistent.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: for example by routing a user to the primary, or to a replica that has caught up, after they write.

options.text: False
options.why: It is a per-client session guarantee and does not need global linearizability.

questions.explanation: Linearizable behaves like one copy with a real-time order. Read-your-writes and monotonic reads are weaker session guarantees that are often enough for user-facing apps.

questions.prompt: Analysts need daily revenue totals by region across several billion rows, touching only three of forty columns. Which setup fits best?

options.text: A columnar warehouse such as Snowflake, fed by a pipeline.
options.why: Right: columnar storage reads only the needed columns and compresses well for scans.

options.text: Run the queries on the primary OLTP Postgres during business hours.
options.why: Long scans compete with transactional traffic and row storage reads whole rows.

options.text: Add a B-tree index on every column of the orders table.
options.why: Indexes do not make full aggregations cheap and they slow every write.

options.text: Cache each report in Redis with a one minute TTL.
options.why: Caching hides repeated reads but the first computation is still a huge scan.

questions.explanation: OLTP serves many small transactions with row storage; OLAP serves large scans and aggregations, where columnar storage, compression and separate compute win.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about pgvector and similarity metrics are correct?

options.text: For vectors normalised to length 1, cosine similarity and inner product rank results identically.
options.why: Right: with unit length the cosine equals the dot product.

options.text: For unit-length vectors, ranking by L2 distance gives the same order as ranking by cosine similarity.
options.why: Right: squared L2 equals 2 minus twice the cosine for unit vectors.

options.text: Cosine similarity ignores vector magnitude and compares only direction.
options.why: Right: it divides by both norms.

options.text: In pgvector the <=> operator computes Euclidean (L2) distance.
options.why: Wrong: <-> is L2, <=> is cosine distance and <#> is negative inner product.

options.text: An HNSW index must be trained on the full dataset before any row is inserted.
options.why: Wrong: training is an IVF concept; HNSW indexes can be built incrementally.

questions.explanation: Pick the metric the embedding model was trained for, and make sure the operator class of the index matches the operator used in the query.

questions.prompt: You must pick an approximate index for a pgvector table that receives continuous inserts and needs high recall at low latency. Which statement guides the choice?

options.text: HNSW usually gives a better speed to recall trade-off but needs more memory and build time.
options.why: Right: the usual choice when recall and latency matter.

options.text: IVFFlat is always more accurate than HNSW because it checks every cluster for every query.
options.why: It probes only some lists, so recall depends on how many it probes.

options.text: Both return exact nearest neighbours, so the choice only affects disk size and nothing else.
options.why: Both are approximate and trade recall for speed.

options.text: IVFFlat needs no data present at build time, while HNSW cannot be built on a populated table.
options.why: Reversed: IVFFlat needs representative data to pick centroids.

questions.explanation: Approximate nearest neighbour indexes trade recall for speed. Tune ef_search for HNSW or probes for IVFFlat, and measure recall against an exact scan.
